content: Copper(II) sulfate, with the chemical formula CuSO₄, is a compound that exists in various hydrated forms. The anhydrous form appears as a pale green or gray-white powder, while the pentahydrate form, which is the most commonly encountered, is bright blue. This hydrated form naturally occurs as the mineral chalcanthite. Historically, copper(II) sulfate has been referred to as blue vitriol or bluestone. Commercially available copper sulfate is typically purchased rather than synthesized in laboratories. However, it can be prepared by reacting sulfuric acid with copper(II) compounds, such as copper(II) oxide. The pentahydrate form decomposes before melting, losing four water molecules at 110°C and all five at 150°C. At 650°C, it further decomposes into copper(II) oxide (CuO) and sulfur trioxide (SO₃). When heated in an open flame, the crystals lose their water content and turn grayish-white. Copper sulfate pentahydrate is widely used as a fungicide. When mixed with lime, it forms Bordeaux mixture, which is effective in controlling fungal infections on crops like grapes, melons, and berries. Another application is the Cheshunt compound, a mixture of copper sulfate and ammonium carbonate, used in horticulture to prevent damping-off in seedlings. As an herbicide, it is employed to manage invasive aquatic plants and plant roots near water pipes. In aquariums, a dilute solution of copper sulfate is used to treat parasitic infections in fish and to eliminate snails, though care must be taken as copper ions are highly toxic to fish. Additionally, copper sulfate is effective in controlling algae growth at very low concentrations and inhibits bacterial growth, including that of E. coli. In analytical chemistry, copper sulfate is used in several tests. It is a component of Fehling's solution and Benedict's solution, which detect reducing sugars by reducing soluble blue copper(II) sulfate to insoluble red copper(I) oxide. It is also used in the Biuret reagent to test for proteins and in blood tests for anemia, where blood is dropped into a copper sulfate solution of known specific gravity. Blood with sufficient hemoglobin sinks rapidly, while blood with lower hemoglobin content floats or sinks slowly. In flame tests, copper ions emit a deep blue-green light, distinct from the flame color of barium. In organic synthesis, anhydrous copper sulfate acts as a catalyst in transacetalization reactions. The hydrated form reacts with potassium permanganate to produce an oxidant for converting primary alcohols. Copper sulfate is commonly included in educational chemistry kits and is used in schools for experiments such as growing crystals and copper plating. Due to its toxicity, it is not recommended for use by young children. It is also used to demonstrate exothermic reactions, such as when steel wool or magnesium ribbon is placed in an aqueous copper sulfate solution. In another educational demonstration, the principle of mineral hydration is illustrated by heating the blue pentahydrate form to produce the white anhydrous form, with water evaporating in the process. Adding water back to the anhydrous compound restores the blue pentahydrate form. A single metal replacement reaction can also be demonstrated by submerging iron in a copper sulfate solution, where iron dissolves and copper precipitates. Copper can also be electroplated onto iron in this process. Other applications of copper sulfate include its use in hair dyes, glass coloring, leather and textile processing, as an ingredient in baby formula milk, and in pyrotechnics as a green colorant.
